description: DevOps engineer and groundwater researcher from the Philippines, taking on “Be an Earth System Trend Detective” with a question close to home: where is Philippine groundwater being depleted, where is it holding steady, and which of those trends are real?
summary:
The UN World Food Programme warns that the 2026–27 El Niño could push at least 49 million more people into acute hunger. When rains fail, farms and towns fall back on groundwater, yet in many places few wells measure it.

Groundwater Storage Trends is a free web app and open API that lets anyone ask whether the water stored underground is rising or falling, for any country, drawn shape or boundary file.

It runs trend detection on NASA’s 2003–2026 water-cycle record: GLDAS-2.2 groundwater estimates, constrained by GRACE satellite gravity data, compared with GPM IMERG rainfall, with El Niño and La Niña months marked. It reports whether storage is changing, whether the direction shifted, whether it follows rainfall, and which regions to look at first. Every answer gives a plain sentence, a slope per decade and a 95% range. The statistics suit slow-changing data, so noise is not mistaken for a trend, and the app warns when a region is too small for the satellites to resolve.

It shows where to look closer and how sure each answer is. It does not forecast drought; its figures are model estimates, not well measurements.
details:
What it does and how it works. Groundwater Storage Trends is a web app with an open REST API behind it. You give it a region (a country, a box or shape you draw, or your own boundary file as GeoJSON or a zipped shapefile) and it runs trend analysis on NASA water-cycle data for that area. Google Earth Engine pulls an area-averaged monthly series from NASA GLDAS-2.2 (groundwater, total water storage, soil moisture, evapotranspiration and runoff, 2003 to 2026) and NASA GPM IMERG (rainfall). All the statistics run in our own service. The app answers four questions. Is storage rising or falling? Did the direction change? Does storage follow rainfall? Which regions should we look at first?

Benefits and intended impact. Groundwater supplies homes and farms, but in many places few wells measure it. Our tool gives water agencies, researchers, students and developers one method that works the same way for every region. Each answer has a verdict in a plain sentence, a slope per decade, a 95% range and a CSV download. We built it for triage. It shows where a closer look with local records is worth the effort.

Tools and software. The API is written in Python 3.13 with FastAPI, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, statsmodels, pymannkendall, piecewise-regression, Shapely and the Earth Engine API. It ships as a Docker image and uses PostgreSQL and Valkey. The web app uses React, TypeScript, Vite and D3. We wrote the code, tests and documents with AI assistance (Anthropic’s Claude, through Claude Code), and we directed and reviewed the work. Every statistic is tested against a number computed another way, and the API’s full check runs 3,194 automated tests.

How it is creative. You choose the region, so the tool is not tied to one country. When a trend cannot be told apart from noise, the app says so and treats that as a result. When a region is smaller than the satellites can resolve, the app warns you and offers a larger region to analyse. The limits of the data go out with the answers they apply to, in the same wording every time.

Factors we considered. The GRACE satellites measure changes in total water storage, not groundwater. Every groundwater figure here is a model’s estimate, not a well measurement. GRACE resolves areas of roughly 150,000 km², so small regions share signal with their neighbours. Groundwater also changes slowly. In our simulations, standard trend tests called trendless noise a trend 28% to 65% of the time, so we use a test that allows for this, and we adjust the results when many regions are tested together. A trend on its own says nothing about cause. The record covers just over two decades, and we found no study that checks these estimates against wells in the Philippines.
